To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the biochemical changes induced by GF intoxication in keratins 18 and 8 could be involved in the signalling pathways that regulate cell death in hepatocytes.

griseofulin treatment of mice induced changes in biochemical properties (solubility and phosphorylation) of K8/8 intermediate filaments and that these changes were associated with hepatocyte apoptosis.
the phosphorylation status of keratins is altered by griseofulvina-induced hepatotoxicity.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of the molecular mechanism of action of keratins, which is essential to the understanding of their protective role in liver diseases and the development of new therapeutic strategies for liver diseases.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms by which keratine intermediate filaments play a role in the protection against chemical-induced toxic stress.
the identification of the mechanisms involved in the protective role played by keratins against chemical injuries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
griseofluvin-induced changes in keratin properties and organisation in the cell could be involved in the modulation of signalling pathways that are important for hepatocyte survival.
griseofulin-induced keratin changes in hepatocytes could play an essential role, at least in part, in the protection of these cells against toxic stress.
the changes in biochemical properties and phosphorylation status of keratin are involved in the protective role of K8/ 18 in hepatocytes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
griseofulin intoxication induces the remodelling and aggregation of keratin intermediate filament proteins which in turn could modify their binding to signalling molecules.

the changes in the physiochemical properties of keratines induced by griseofulvicn intoxication could be a mechanism by which keratin intermediate filamenets play their role in protecting hepatocytes against chemical stress.
keratins are involved in the protection of liver cells from chemical injuries by regulating the signalling pathways in response to stress.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the formation of Mallary-Denk bodies in response to griseofulvic intoxication is a consequence of the remodelling and reorganisation of intermediate filament proteins, which is associated with changes in keratin phosphorylation and solubility.
the phosphorylation of specific keratin epitopes could be involved in the regulation of keratin function and in the remodellings of the cytoskeleton that occur in response to stress in hepatocytes.
keratins 18 and 8 are not only involved in the protection of the cell from mechanical stress, but also from chemical stress.
